utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Can we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, Mark Harmon, and Ms. Inger du Ru for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. And good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. For the Defence, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Daniela Tasic, Gregor Guy-Smith, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Saxon, who are we hearing today?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Mr. Rade Raseta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Rade Raseta.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I was born in Donji Lapac, the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I'm Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you retired now?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was your profession?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I completed the secondary non-commissioned officer school. I also completed education for -- for officers, and I became a second lieutenant, and I worked as a non-commissioned officers in the army, and then I was accepted in the security service in JNA, and I completed the school for security in 1976 [Realtime transcript read in error "1996"], after which I was the chief of security in units at the rank of regiment brigade. And then I was a desk officer and Deputy Chief in the security service of the infantry division. And I was also an officer in counter-intelligence and Deputy Chief of counter-intelligence of the counter-intelligence group. I was also the chief of information and analysis in the security department of the army. And then, after I was transferred to the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, I was also chief of information and analysis section in the security department. And then I was the chief of security of the Main Staff of the army -- of the Serbian army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Initially, were you serving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I heard no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have an error in line 4 on page 3 of the transcript. I think the year is mistakenly stated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you very much, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Raseta, initially were you serving in the Yugoslav People's Army, or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry again, Mr. Saxon. What I did say that it was -- it is supposed to be 1976; it is still not typed. So you've got to make sure it's -- because 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At line 4, page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. That's what it should be. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some point did the JNA change its name?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. It changed its name to the army of the federal republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And approximately when was that; do you know? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This was in 1992 or 1993; I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you then continue to serve as an officer in the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The 1st of January, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And from which army did you retire?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: From the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I returned, I went back and then for a few months, I was in the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I mean here in 1995. That same year, I requested to retire, and I was retired in 1996, the 1st of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We'll get along probably more quickly, Mr. Raseta, if you could just answer the question that I ask you. So can we say that you retired from the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you worked in the security services after 1976. In general terms, what kind of work did the security organs of the JNA and the VJ do? What was their focus?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The main role of the security organ, or the security service of the JNA, and then later on, in the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is counter-intelligence protection of commands, units, and institutions against foreign intelligence services, extreme immigration, terrorism and diversions. Also, prevention and discovery of theft of ammunition, equipment, and other significant assets for the armed forces. And then issuing various measures of security for the planning of staffs and units, and cooperation with similar services, related services, and mainly that would have been the focus of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And tell us, how would the work of the security organs differ from the work of the intelligence organs, just in general terms?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Intelligence organs, their main role was discovery and following the intentions of foreign armed forces in all the matters dealing with aggression against one's country and following their intelligence services. The security service had a different role. It was to protect, as counter-intelligence commands and units and areas of their responsibility, to protect them against infiltration by foreign intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I forgot to ask you a question. When you retired, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, where did you serve between October 1993 and August 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I served in the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to October of that year, October of 1993, where were you posted?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I was posted as chief of information and analysis in the security department of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And again that was the 3rd Army of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where was the 3rd Army based at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It was based in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time, prior to October 1993, who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: My superior was Colonel Kuzmanovic, Petar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And prior to October 1993, how was your relationship with Colonel Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It was official.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Did anything -- anything special happen to your relationship with Colonel Kuzmanovic prior to October?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, circumstances were such that Colonel Kuzmanovic, who was from the territory of Republika Srpska, and I suppose that you assume that he actually tried to rally us, all of us who were from Republika Srpska, to go -- to go back to our home country and participant in the Defence of those lands. On one occasion I actually objected to his comments. I said that he was right, and that as a chief of service, he is the one who should lead us and take us there because that is where he belonged just as we did. But I he didn't like that. And on the first occasion that presented itself when an order from the General Staff came, that a number of officers had to be sent to the Republic of Serbian Krajina, he added my name to that order and said --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Colonel, let's just take this step by step, okay? Good. So at some point after you had this discussion with Colonel Kuzmanovic, you said that an order came from the General Staff. Which General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in general terms what did this order say? What was it about?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That order said that a group of officers, and there was a list of names there, should be sent -- transferred to the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. An order was issued for subordinate commands to regulate the transfer of service to transport them to Belgrade and to appoint our deputies, or their deputies in their place, and if the occasion presents itself that we should return at some later point to our old duties. There was also specified a time when we should leave and what the manner of our transport there would be and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarification on two points, Mr. Saxon. Sir, you say this Colonel Kuzmanovic said you -- all of you who came from Republika Srpska should go back to your home country and participate in the defence of those lands. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said you were born in Donji Lapac, in Croatia. Now why were you required to go to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Not Republika Srpska, but the Republic of Serbian Krajina, because Donji Lapac is part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, its territory belongs there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Does it mean where at page 6, line 21, it refers to all of you who come from Republika Srpska, was that a mistake in -- either by you or by the interpreter? Can you see that, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Refers to Republika Srpska, not the RSK. So you say those of you who come from the RSK must go back there. Is that what it said -- what you were saying? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can be helpful. The witness did say Republika Srpska, as far as I could hear, but I think when he said that, he meant Colonel Kuzmanovic, who was from Republika Srpska, because there were officers from both those lands. But what he said was correctly recorded in the transcript. So it is possible that there were officers from both those territories, and maybe that's something that can be cleared up with the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would have to be because the record doesn't clearly say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you like me to clarify this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could, please. And if, indeed, he meant that people from Republika Srpska must go to Republika Srpska, and the people from the RSK must go to the RSK, and that he was then expected to go to the RSK, then that clears my next point. But can we clear whether that was indeed the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Going back to this point, Colonel, during this discussion with Colonel Kuzmanovic, how many people were present, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: There were four or five people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were there -- were these persons present from just the Republika Srpska, just the Republika Srpska Krajina, or from both territories?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I was from the Republic of Serbian Krajina; whereas, Kuzmanovic was from Republika Srpska, and the others were from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So previously, when you described this conversation with Colonel Kuzmanovic, and this is at line 20 of page 6, and you described him as "who was from the territory of Republika Srpska. And I suppose that you assumed that he actually tried to rally us, all of us who were from Republika Srpska." Did you mean to only include Republika Srpska in that statement, or did you mean to be more inclusive and include Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I think I will clarify this. Just as we from the Republic of Serbian Krajina officers were sent to the Serbian Krajina temporarily, in the same manner, the officers from Republika Srpska were sent to that territory, to the Serbian Republic. So there should be no difference between those two groups, not just those who were from the Republic of Serbian Krajina should be sent to their land but also the others. So there was the same need, and they, too, were sent to Republika Srpska. So he, too, based on this sort of homeland patriotism should have been sent to his home land. I don't know if I have clarified this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's sufficient for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have, sir. But where were you when this discussion was taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What I want to know is in which territory, in which republic were you when you were going told you have got to be transferred to the RSK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the Republic of Serbia, in Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Going back to this order that you mentioned, and you mentioned that one of the things the order said was that there was a list of names there and a group of officers should be transferred to the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Can you recall whether the order mentioned a time-period, for how long were the officers supposed to be transferred to the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Up to one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And you also told the Chamber that the order was issued for subordinate commands to regulate the transfer of service, to transport them to Belgrade. And then you said: "And to appointed our deputies or their deputies in their place." Can you explain what you meant by that, just a little bit more clearly?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: This General Staff order contained also provision that the officers who were transferred for temporary duty to Serbian Krajina, that they should be released of their duties, that their deputies should be appointed in their positions, and that they should be taken by bus to Belgrade, where we all gathered from the then-Republic of Yugoslavia, to the second garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel, again, I just want to take this one step at a time, all right? Before we go any further, I just want to clarify one point. Initially, or originally, when this order came from the General Staff to the 3rd Army, was your name on it?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was subsequently added by Colonel Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you have a discussion with Colonel Kuzmanovic as to how it came about that he added your name?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. And he explained to me that I was omitted -- my name was omitted by error, and that he had consulted the chief of the Security Administration who agreed that my name should also be on the list in this order, and that's how it was added. That's how my name was added.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you refer to the chief of the Security Administration, at that time, who was that, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It was Colonel General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did General Dimitrijevic have any relationship with the General Staff of the VJ, or was the Security Administration part of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was part of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And before we go on with what happened with this order that affected you, do you know anyone in the army of Yugoslavia at the time, or at that approximate time, who refused such an order to serve in the army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a Lieutenant-Colonel Jovan Svjilar [phoen]. He refused to go for health reasons because he had -- his family lived in Skopje. His request was granted, but he was expelled from the security service, and he was appointed to some desk officer service outside of our service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to this order to which your name was added, how much time passed before your order -- this order was implemented approximately?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Not that long, 10 to 15 days, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you describe, briefly, initially how was your transport to the SVK organised? What was the first step?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The first step was at the indicated time from the order the transport was supposed to start, and all of us from the 3rd Army were grouped in Nis. And from there, we were transferred to Belgrade by bus, and at the centre of the high military schools, we all assembled from all the garrisons of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We were all placed in one hall Colonel Stevo Medakovic, I think at the time he was chief of the 40th [Realtime transcript read in error "4th"] Personnel Centre, did the roll-call.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I stop you for a minute. Before we going on to what Colonel Medakovic did, you referred -- you said all of us from the 3rd Army were grouped in Nis. Approximately how many officers or men from the 3rd Army went up to Belgrade, subject to this order, that went to that high military school, I should say?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: About 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the centre of the high military school, do you recall where that centre was located?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: In Banjica, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to Colonel Medakovic, you mentioned that he did the roll-call, and what, if anything, did Colonel Medakovic do or say after that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: After the roll-call, he informed all of us who were there that we were going to the command of the Main Staff of the army of the Serbian Krajina in Knin, that we were going to go there by bus, that the road was safe, that we shouldn't be thinking about that. That they are going to deal with all of our status issues there once -- after we are deployed. That we would be deployed, all of us, to the Main Staff command on different duties, depending on what our profession and speciality was. And after that, we were going to fill in certain documents that the personnel organ of the Main Staff command would collate and forward to the 40th Personnel Centre, so that all of us, who were sent to the army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina would receive the benefits that were due to us, such as our salary, the appropriate payment category groups, and that everything would be dealt with properly that arises from our transfer to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to clarify one point in the record. You said that one of the things that Colonel Medakovic said was - and this is written in English - "that they will be deal with all of our status issues there once -- after we are deployed." When you say "they will deal with all of our status issues," who is "they"? Who are you referring to by "they"?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The 40th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And if I can just note that at page 13, line 9, I believe the witness said 40th, not 4th, in the record right now it says 4th. And after Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have a slight problem again in the translation, page 14, line 11, when the witness said -- he said transfer, premestaj. And in English this word was translated as position. So I'm questioning the interpreters, if this is the adequate term for the word premestaj. He said practically, yes, transfer, practically. The end of the transfer is from our position. That's what he said -- from our transfer, from our position does not seem adequate to what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do not want to pretend to understand what you are saying, Mr. Lukic. I'm completely at a loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I heard is that when the witness spoke in Serbian he said do naseg premestaj, and that is the end of his sentence, until our transfer. In the English it should state, up to our transfer, full point. And then this part, to that position, I did not hear him say that in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's -- it's an interpretation thing. You have to deal with the interpreters with that now. I don't think anyone of us here can help, except the interpreter. What did you hear, madam interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Well, he -- perhaps the witness can repeat, Your Honour, or we can listen to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat himself, please, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel, a few moments ago you described what Colonel Medakovic told the group of officers in the hall of the military centre, the education centre. And at the end of your response, you gave the following long sentence, and it's the end of this sentence that I'd like you to focus on, but I will read the entire sentence: "And after that we were going to fill in certain documents that the personnel organ of the Main Staff command would" - could late, I don't know what that was suppose to be - "and forward to the 40th Personnel Centre so that all of us, who were sent to the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, would receive the benefits that were due to us, such as our salary, the appropriate payment category groups ..." And this is the line that is being discussed. What we have in English is: "And that ... would be dealt with properly that arises from our transfer to that position." That last point as I've just relayed it back to you, does it correctly state what you were trying to express at the end of that response?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I see Mr. Lukic has thrown in the towel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sure he'll rise again, Your Honour. He always does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After -- if can you recall, approximately how many officers were gathered in that hall or meeting room, when Colonel Medakovic was speaking? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: About 50 or 60 officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were about 20 officers from the 3rd Army, which was based in Nis. Where were the other officers coming from; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. There were people from all garrisons and the -- they were from the command units from the air force and -- but I really couldn't say. I think they were also from the land forces. But I couldn't really say exactly who.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And how, then, were you and your colleagues transported to the SVK? Actually, first of all, I should ask: Where specifically were you going to be taken? What town or city?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the witness said Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How were you and your colleagues transported to Knin?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: By bus. But I don't know if there was one bus or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind of buses were they?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Military buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall who sat next to you on the bus that took to you Knin?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Mladen Karan, he is now a retired colonel, was sitting next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know prior to serving in the SVK, where was Mladen Karan serving?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I think that he was in the air force and in the anti-aircraft defence. Of course, in the security section.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know what position Mladen Karan then subsequently took up with the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: You mean when we came to the army of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He was appointed to the post of chief of security in the Kordun Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P1865, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, Colonel Raseta, that this document is an order from the 3rd Army command dated the 7th of October, 1994. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there is -- it starts off with an order on the transfer an appointment to the 40th Personnel Centre, and then we see a series of names. Below that we see a reference to -- there's a paragraph below the number 8. And it -- it says: "All the above mentioned professional soldiers have to report to the centre of the military schools of the Yugoslav army in the Belgrade garrison ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I have lost the -- just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I could show you on my hard copy, with the usher's assistance, if that would make things easier.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I see it. I see it, yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was this the same centre of military schools that you were taken to prior to going to the army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Down below that we see a second part of this order to initiate procedure for termination of professional military service.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what, if anything, does this document -- does this order demonstrate to you?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It demonstrates -- well, it's not -- what's in the points 1 to 8 is not in dispute, to send people to the army of the Serbian Krajina. But then there is a list of senior officers to initiate procedure for termination of professional military service, because they refused to carry out the order of transfer to the army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does that, in your mind, demonstrate anything else?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't know what you're thinking of. The proceedings were initiated for refusal to execute an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. We can leave this document now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If Your Honours are ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon, against the names of 1 to 8 there's a little sentence at the end which says, "... did not follow a transfer order." Do you see that? Look at number 8, number 7, number 6, number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Almost all of them. What, if any, significance can drawn from that, Mr. Witness? Does it mean these eight people did not go on transfer to the army of the Republic of the -- Srpska Krajina? Did you hear me, sir, or did you get any interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry, I didn't understand. Were you addressing me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was asking if -- actually, I was asking what it means to say that the officers 1 to 8 did not follow a transfer order. Does it mean they didn't go to the -- to the army of the Republika of Srpska Krajina; or what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means that they had already been ordered to transfer to the army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. And for various reasons, some justified, some not, they did not carry out the order, so this is another order to send them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if you see number 1 and number 2, they say they deliberately left units of the 40th Personnel Centre. Now, if they deliberately left, they cannot be available to get a second transfer, can they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a matter that exceeds my knowledge, but let's assume that these were people who deserted and the people who did not respond, the army command took another -- made another attempt to order them to go to the army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. Perhaps this is the last attempt before possibly making other steps or carrying out some sanctions. There are two categories here: Those who left; and those who did not respond. So there are two types of cases here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But I'm not quite sure how you make that difference. If you say they deliberately left the units of the 40th Personnel Centre and some say -- are said to -- did not follow a transfer order. To me, doesn't look like -- these are two different meanings. And those who left the Personnel Centre cannot then be available to be subject to this second order, because they've left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this implies that those who left the units, they returned to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and now the command here wanted to include them in the order, those who left the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina of their own will and those who did not respond to the 40th Personnel Centre, so this is another attempt with this order to send them to the Serbian army of the Krajina. I think that's how it is. I can't see any other interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That's for your effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel, following up on His Honour's questions, while you were serving in the SVK, were you aware of persons who left the 40th Personnel Centre and tried to return to their former duties in the army of Yugoslavia? Did such situations occur?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: But these were individual cases mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We can leave this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel, when you arrived in the SVK, in Knin, who gave you your assignment there?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: My assignment was given to me by Colonel Dimitrijevic, who was the chief of the Main Staff security section at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The confusion about the last name which is quite important, page 21, line 23 -- line 22, the witness mentioned a different last name. I think perhaps we could clear it up by saying that it was the person from the Main Staff. Mr. Saxon really wanted to clear that up. Perhaps the witness could slowly repeat the last name of that colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, could you slowly repeat the last name of the colonel in the SVK who gave you your assignment in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. It is Colonel Vuk Dmitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if any organ of the SVK informed other organs about your assignment and the assignments of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you arrived in Knin, you received an assignment within the SVK, and would it be fair to say that your other colleagues from the VJ also received their assignments at that time? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the SVK inform anyone from the VJ about the assignments that had been made, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. Certain documents and forms were filled in for those of us newly arrived. This is something that was all assembled together by the personnel organ and sent to the 40th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Do you know why that was done?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, it was done in order for us to receive our benefits, to receive the salaries that were commensurate with the regulations. You had to assume duty, fill in the form, send that to the 40th Personnel Centre, and then I assumed that the 40th Personnel Centre sent that to the accounting centre, where our salaries were calculated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. What was -- well, since you mention the topic of salaries, just so that the record is clear, who was it who paid your salary while you were serving in the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, did you personally receive your salary?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I did not receive it personally. A member of my family received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And in what republic or territory was that family member who received your salary?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. While you were serving in the SVK, was your salary the same as it was when you were serving in the VJ 3rd Army, prior to October 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. It was slightly increased by about 15 per cent, because of -- as a hardship allowance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you leave the Yugoslav army in order to serve in the SVK, or did you remain in the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I was transferred to the SVK, and I had all the insignia of the SVK, and I was a member of the SVK at the time, while I was serving in that army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But I guess my question was: Did you leave the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how one can interpret that. I was a member of the army of Yugoslavia, but I was temporarily assigned to duty in the SVK. So practically I was a member of the army of Yugoslavia, temporarily assigned to the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is 65 ter 536, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, this document is from the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina, dated the 10th of December, 1994. And you see it is addressed to the General Staff of the Yugoslav army, to the personnel administration of the 40th Personnel Centre. Do you see that, towards the top?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then below that it says: "Due to the unresolved situation in the service, we are kindly asking you to issue orders on the appointment of the following professional officers ..." And then below that we see a list of names, a list of officers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we just briefly go to the last page, please, in both languages. And if we could focus on the last paragraph which perhaps could be enlarged in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That last paragraph says: "The above-named were already put forward for appointment as Generals by the decree of the President of the Republic. In case it is not feasible, we are kindly asking for the above-named to be appointed, according to the above-listed proposals."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, that first sentence towards the top that refers to the unresolved situation in the service, are you aware of what that unresolved situation was? And, if so, can you explain it to us, briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I object to the formulation of this question. I would appreciate it if the Prosecutor asked the witness whether he knows, because this is a fact witness, whether he knows -- whether he is familiar with these facts, because he was not called here as an expert witness. So if there's something to clarify, it should first be clarified whether he is familiar or aware of these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in my own terms, I believe I did that in my question. I asked the witness about there sentence that refers to an unresolved situation, and I asked the witness whether he was aware of what that unresolved situation was, which is a factual question. And then I asked: "If so, can you explain it to us?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see that's at page 25, line 4. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, Colonel? What was that unresolved situation involving these officers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First of all, were you aware of this unresolved situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of this, but now, looking at this document, I -- it sort of refreshed my memory as to what this refers to. Because these are officers that I know, most of them, except for one person, and I know that there were some vacant posts, vacant establishment posts, that these officers were supposed to be appointed to, and the staff commander is sending this document to the 40th Personnel Centre, proposing that these officers be appointed to those vacant establishment posts. And this was actually acted upon, because I know that all of these officers were actually appointed to these posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the fact -- you mention these vacant establishment posts. Why was it important for the officers -- let me step back for one moment. When you refer to "vacant posts," or vacant establishment posts," vacant posts where?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, for instance if we take number one, we see that it is about Dusan Loncar, son of Mitar. He was supposed to be the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the SVK, because his predecessor, Vojislav [as interpreted] Djukic, was transferred to a position in the Yugoslav army so that his position remained vacant and then followed this order to appoint him to that position, and a similar situation is true of the other persons who are mentioned here. And if you would like me to, I can explain each individual case. But in any case, it was a similar procedure as in the case of Dusan Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why would it be important, for example, sticking with the case of Dusan Loncar, why would it be important to be placed on that vacant establishment post of the 40th Personnel Centre? What effect would that have? What impact would that have?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Up until then, he was in the 11th, East Slovenia Corps. I think he was a Chief of Staff there. But I'm not sure, I can't remember at this point. But in view of his abilities and his qualifications, he was the primary candidate to be appointed to this post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But my question is something different. Once an officer like Dusan Loncar is appointed to that vacant post, what would be the consequences of that? What, if any, consequences would be there, for example, on the benefits or entitlements or other matters received from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, of course, he would have more benefits and more entitlements, because this would be a higher position. And, of course, a higher position would have higher benefits and everything else. I don't want to repeat myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2333, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we leave this exhibit, Colonel, you mentioned there was one officer on this list who you did not know. Can we turn -- Is that officer listed on the first page, or should we turn to the next page?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I think it is on the second -- the last page. It was the last person on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So it was Colonel Boro Poznanovic, who you did not know; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could leave that document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, when you served in the SVK, what uniform did you wear?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I wore the uniform of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia army member, but the insignia that I wore were the insignia of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did all of the officers coming from the VJ to the SVK wear the SVK insignia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: There were some exceptions. I think the battalion commander, the police commander, Stevo Subotic, he wore the insignia of a member of the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And I recall a situation when the then president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Mr. Hadzic, came to his unit, and when he reported to him, the President was satisfied with the inspection and so on, but he objected to his not having the insignia of the army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina on his cap, but, rather of those of Yugoslavia. And he answered, Well, when you start paying for my salary, I will start wearing your insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: First of all, can you repeated the last name of this commander, this person named Stevo.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Commander -- battalion commander Stevo Subotic. He was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In your last response you referred to Commander Subotic first as battalion commander and then you said the police commander; can you explain that? What was his unit?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He was a commander of a police battalion in the command of the Main Staff of the Serbian Krajina army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you present when this exchange between Mr. Hadzic and Commander Subotic occurred?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I was not present myself, but Captain Subotic told me about it. And because I was the most senior officer in the security department at the time, that's why he informed me of it, but I also confirmed this with his -- or actually, I checked this with his officers, his superior officers who were there themselves, who were present during this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. Would this be the right moment for the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we return briefly to what is now Exhibit P2333.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel Raseta, we looked at this document shortly before we took our break, and just so the record is clear, I just want to clarify a point or two, this document signed by General Celeketic from the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina. When this document was -- was produced, the officers who are mentioned here, where physically were they serving at that time? In which army?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: They were serving in the army of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and so, for example, if we look at number 2, Lazo Babic, it says duty: "VJ, 40th Personnel Centre." And then it says, "18th Corps commander." Was that the position that Mr. Babic was performing at that time in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. Colonel Lazo Babic was the Chief of Staff at the 18th Corps and Major-General Celeketic at the time was the commander, the corps commander. When General Celeketic was appointed as commander of the Main Staff of the Serbian army of Krajina, the proposal was drafted for Lazo Babic to replace him and to be appointed as commander of the 39th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm just confused, because the duty here under Mr. Babic refers to the 18th Corps. Why did you -- why did you refer to the 39th Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: My apologies. I made a total error in numbering that corps. It's actually the 18th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can leave this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel, while you served in the SVK, did you receive any money from the SVK or from the RSK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. While you served in the SVK, did you receive any extra allowances from the VJ, from the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No. Except for the 15 per cent which was -- that I have already mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned before that the VJ continued to pay the salaries and benefits of the -- of many of the officers who were serving in the SVK. Was it important for the SVK that the VJ paid the salaries and benefits of many of the officers serving in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this question calls for the witness to speculate, whether this was important for the SVK. I think that the witness should reply exactly for whom this was important, not for which institution, because he can only testify as to facts that he knows. Except, unless he had some knowledge that related to some institutional knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, clearly this witness can only testify to what he knows. Having said that, this witness was a member of the Main Staff of the SVK, so I submit there is nothing wrong with this question. The witness can answer it, if he knows the answer. And if he does not, he can say, I don't know or I can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that sense, I think that the question was not precise enough. I think he should -- the question should be whether this witness has any information, in view of his post, based on the information that he received while he was in that post. That's the only way that this witness can be framed and not framing it by providing an answer for the SVK in general. I think that this question, the way it is put, is of a global nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness can answer the question, he can then explain what the basis for his response and knowledge is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shouldn't we do it the other way around, lay a foundation for the question. You say he was in the Main Staff of the SVK. Just lay that foundation and then put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel, at some point, did you -- step back for a minute. What were you assigned to do when you first came to the SVK? What was your first assignment?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, I was to take over the duty that I was appointed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what that duty was? Refresh our memory.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The chief of information and analysis within the security department of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you -- how long did you carry out that duty?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: For about a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so by then -- in the autumn of 1994, did you receive another position?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: On 19th December, 1994, I was appointed to the duty of chief of the security department of the Main Staff of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for how long did you carry out that position?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Until August 14th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during that time, were you a member of the Main Staff of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I was a member of the Main Staff of the SVK from the moment I arrived at the Main Staff of the SVK. And when I was promoted to the position of chief of the security department of the Main Staff, I was one of the commanders assistants and one of his closest associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who was that commander? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The commander's name was Colonel General Milan Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to repeat the question that I asked you earlier. If you know, was it important for the SVK that the VJ paid the salaries and benefits of many of the officers serving in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I do not have detailed information about that, nor did I ever take part in any discussions relating to that matter. But if you want my personal opinion, I can give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is a fact witness, and that's what he was called here to do, to testify to the facts that he has knowledge of, and he said himself that he doesn't have any knowledge relating to these facts, and this is really calling for speculation. He can only provide his own opinion but not to give an answer regarding an institution, because he said that he cannot really -- and even as a fact witness, he cannot actually speculate and give his own opinions. He can only speak of the facts that he knows, and everything else would be speculation, and he came here, again, as a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was it important to you, Witness, serving in the SVK that the VJ paid your salary and benefits?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: For me, it was actually irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. While you served in the SVK, what was the arrangement for food and accommodation for officers who had come from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: The food was provided by the Main Staff of the SVK, and the same is true for accommodation. We had a -- we used the premises of a leased hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you give us an idea of how many VJ officers assigned to the 40th Personnel Centre, including yourself, were serving in command positions in the SVK while you were there in 1993, 1994, and 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I cannot provide the precise information, but I think there were about 100 to 120 officers in the entire SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you provide a figure, even an approximate figure, of what percentage of those officers serving in the SVK had come from the VJ office -- had come from the VJ, through the 40th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I really couldn't give you a number. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Of these 100 to 120 officers that you mentioned, do you know whether all of these officers were originally from the territory of the RSK or not?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly they originated from there, but there was some other ethnic members. There was one Muslim; there was one Macedonian that I know of; I think one who was an ethnic Croat who happened to be in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And their wives were from that area, so they remained on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know where General Celeketic was from?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: General Celeketic was born in Vojvodina, near Indjija someplace near Indjija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I have some names of persons that I'd like to give you. And I'd like to ask you, as I read each name, whether while you served in the SVK, whether you knew these persons. I'll start with Colonel General Mile Mrksic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the Main Staff after Celeketic was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you recall the first time that you saw Mrksic in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him sometime in the spring of 1995, when he was in the territory of the Serbian Krajina, together with Colonel General of the air force, Ljubisa Velickovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was this before General Mrksic took up his duties as commander of the SVK or after?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Before he became the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you referred to Colonel General of the air force, Ljubisa Velickovic, to what army or air force did Velickovic belong to at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: General Velickovic was the commander of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence of the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And can you recall where you saw General Mrksic and General Velickovic in early -- in the spring of 1995? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That day I had counselling session or an advisory session that day at the command of the Kordun Corps, and during the work they were brought into the conference room by Colonel Veljko Bosanac the commander of the corps, and he introduced them, and they very briefly stayed there. And one of my senior officers asked General Velickovic the following question: Since Colonel Bosanac said that they were reconnoitring the air space in case of some incursions in order to have the best possible defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, General Velickovic answered that officer of mine that the skies under the Serbian Krajina is the same as the sky above the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Moving on, did you know while you served in the SVK, know of Major-General Borisav Djukic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What position did General Djukic hold in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: When I came to the SVK, the chief of the Main Staff of the SVK was General Borisav Vukic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was it Vukic or Djukic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Dj, Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- going back to General Mrksic, do you know whether General Mrksic, when he served in the SVK, was a member of the 40th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about General Djukic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: I don't understand. Was he a member of the 40th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yes. While he served in the SVK, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He had the same status as I did, and all of us who served in the Serbian army of the Krajina, if that's what you're thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, but that you mean which status?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That he was on the records of the 40th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. How about a gentleman named Lieutenant-Colonel Dragan Saric. Did you know him while you served in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. But it is not Saric but Sarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me, and I apologise for my poor pronunciation of Serbian names. What position did Sarac hold in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: When I came to the security Department of The Main Staff, he was the Deputy Chief of the security department of the Main Staff, the deputy to Colonel Vuk Dimitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know a man named lieutenant-colonel Dusan Smiljanic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. Not lieutenant-colonel, but colonel Dusan Smiljanic. He came to the SVK together with me, and he was assigned as chief of the counter-intelligence group in the Main Staff security Department of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Colonel Kosta Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Kosta Novakovic for a time was the assistant for morale of the Main Staff of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know a man named General Mirko Bjelanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. Not Milanovic, but General Mirko Bjelanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. What was his position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: He was the Main Staff assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Ilija Slavkovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. Only by first and last name. And I know that he was in the Main Staff logistics, but I don't know exactly what post he was carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel, did you know a man named Stoja Spanovic [phoen] while you served in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Did you know a man named Colonel Milan Djilas?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to the Krajina, he was the commander of the 7th Corps, and later he was the chief of artillery at the Main Staff of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll move on to another topic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do, I just -- I know this is maybe a silly question to ask, but I must ask it nonetheless. Were all the members of the army of the SVK members of the 40th Personnel Centre or only some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the precise information about that. But in view of the work that was under way in that connection, I believe that they were all registered at the 40th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The entire army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But only the senior officers who were transferred from the FRY to the SVK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was: Was the entire army members of the 40th Personnel Centre or only some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about the others, but I know about these ones, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Following up on your last response, when you refer to "these ones," are you referring to the officers whose names I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We were talking about them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions about your duties within the security department of the SVK. Can you briefly describe what your duties were, first, as the head of the information analysis section, and subsequently as head of the entire security services of the SVK Main Staff? In general terms.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. The purpose of the information analysis section is that all the information, incoming and outgoing, went through my sector. They were processed, estimated, evaluated. We wrote reports about that and sent them to those in charge, and these reports were signed by the chief of the intelligence department of the Main Staff. This is the answer to this first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just let me just get -- Why do you as chief of security analysis have your reports signed by the chief of the intelligence and not chief of the security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would receive some of those documents that had some things in common, so we had to organise some form of cooperation, and that is why certain documents were given to us for our information and use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you said you wrote reports and sent those to those in charge, and these reports were signed by the chief of the intelligence. I'm talking about documents that are generated by you, not that you receive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Perhaps it was a slip. Perhaps I said it. I didn't say that they were signed by the chief of the intelligence sector but the chief of the security sector of the Main Staff. He was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Saxon, if you look at page 39 from line 23 to page 40, line 3, just maybe you want to clarify that with your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Colonel, in the English translation of your previous answer you were discussing the purpose of the information analysis section, and you said: "We wrote reports about that and sent those ... in charge, and these reports were signed by the chief of the intelligence department of the Main Staff." Do you want to correct that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: It's a total mistake. The chief of the security department, not the intelligence department. It should say the chief of the security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how about your duties when you became head of the security department in the SVK Main Staff? What were your duties then, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I was the chief of the service and handled all the subordinates, security organs and the sections within the security department of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. When you became chief of the security department of the SVK, in an operational sense, who was your direct superior?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: My immediate and only superior was the commander of the Main Staff, Lieutenant -- Colonel General Milan Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As part of your normal duties, did you report to General Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Absolutely, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While you were chief of the security department of the SVK, did you ever report to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. I submitted reports about certain questions to the chief of the Security Administration of the Main Staff of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, in the English transcript it says, "chief of the Security Administration of the Main Staff of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Did you mean to use the term "Main Staff"?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: General Staff. Instead of the Main Staff, the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And why did you submit reports about certain matters to General Dimitrijevic? Can you explain it in relatively simple terms.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the fact that the security service of the SVK used all instructions, all the rules, all special operational and technical means and cadres from the security of the General Staff of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I had the duty, pursuant to all the applicable special measures and special measures as regulated by all our regulations, to report regularly to the Security Administration of the General Staff of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. In addition to reporting to General Dimitrijevic, did you also inform General Dimitrijevic about events?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: We should differentiate here between the following: One thing is to submit reports. These were specific persons from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who were sent for temporary service to the Serbian Krajina and who were there under the operative treatment of the service. So, these people still had to be included in the operative work in the SVK. So this is one line of reporting, which went through our formalised channels of reporting. That was one thing and that was part of my duties. My other duty was to inform the Security Administration if possibly in the territory some problems cropped up that directly jeopardized the security of the commands' units or their operations and which would have negative consequences. In such cases I would report to General Dimitrijevic. However, these reports that I mentioned last occurred very infrequently, I perhaps sent five or six such reports, whereas the other reports about specific persons that -- they were send very frequently. In order to be more clear, the security department here, the security service in the SVK had its rules, its own instructions, its operational and technical means, its cadres, its schools and other elements. Had we had these things, I would be independent of the same service of the FRY, except for just like in the case of all the services, sometimes we would exchange information and have other forms of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to try to clarify a couple of things that you just said to make sure that I understand and that record is clear. In the beginning of your last response - this is on page 42, starting at line 20, continuing to line 25 - you said: "There were specific persons from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who were sent for temporary service to the Serbian Krajina and who were there under the operative treatment of the service." Stopping right there, which service are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: To be even clearer, these were persons who had dossiers up there, and they were sent to the Serbian army of the Krajina with the dossiers so we had to continue our work, in relation to them. So not for them to be in the service but for the service to keep following them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So these were persons who -- these were VJ personnel who had been sent to the SVK who were, if I can put it this way, already under the eye of the security organs of the VJ. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That leaves me a little perplexed. So your security responsibilities included spying on your own colleagues, if I may put it that crudely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which colleagues you're thinking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question to you which you just said yes to from the lawyer there, was: "All right" -- wait a minute, I'm going to tell you what the question was. Okay, "So these were persons who -- these were VJ personnel who had been sent to the SVK who were, if I can put it this way, already under the eye of the security organs of the VJ." So that's saying it elegantly what I said crudely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not espionage in terms of those people. Espionage is something else. We combine the methods and means of work in order to continue to follow them and document any eventual activity of theirs in the territory and in the units. This is what was in the rules and the instructions. This was something that I had to do. I was not making it up myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you were documenting and following your colleagues, fellow personnel, 40th Personnel members who were in the SVK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I considered my colleagues to be members of the security organs. These were my most immediate colleagues. These were my comrades, superiors, just like any others. Yes, I understand that you said that I was actually spying on my colleagues in the security organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when I say "you," I'm not personalizing it. I'm not talking about you. I'm saying was it one of the duties of the security department to spy on 40th Personnel who were with you in the Krajina? That's what you said yes to when -- when Mr. Saxon asked you the question. And I just want to be sure that's what you're saying, that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's only a difference between us in the terms we use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a very small number of such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But what did you do about this small number? When you say you were following them, what does "following them" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Keeping track of them, following them is one of the methods. But we also used other methods that we had at or disposal. In other words, there they were being processed in operational terms. Now, whether -- what other methods there were, I don't think I should discuss that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Colonel, that part of your duties was to monitor the activities of these personnel? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was that because of a concern that these personnel might do something that would be harmful to the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, not only to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but also the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so I can understand, the information that -- obtained from the activities that we've just been discussing, would that be the subject, for example, of your reporting to General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: That's right. Exclusively. I would be reporting exclusively to him regarding these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And what other kind of matters might you report to General Dimitrijevic about, for example?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Well, I can give you an example. For instance, during the election in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the candidates in the election were the late Milan Babic, and President Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you make this very brief.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The -- Babic won the election and Martic lost. However, President Milosevic was not pleased with the outcome, so he ordered directly. This went via Milosevic-Martic. He ordered that these elections be cancelled, and that a new election be organised. And in this new election Martic won. So I reported on this particular situation. And why did I do that?
